title: Monte Rio Redwoods Park Expands for Mountain Biking Recreation
summary:
A rugged Monte Rio refuge quadrupled in size last year, offering nearly 30 miles of trails lovingly maintained by an all-volunteer local cycling association.

The post Monte Rio Redwoods Park Expands for Mountain Biking Recreation appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
If you favor fat-tire biking and seek epic singletrack through postcard stands of Sequoia, head for Monte Rio Redwoods Park and Open Space Preserve. That rugged west county refuge quadrupled in size a year ago when Sonoma County Regional Parks acquired, from Save the Redwoods League, a 1,517-acre parcel laced with nearly 30 miles of trails. It was built and maintained for decades by members of the Gianni Cycling Association, named for the beloved Occidental bike shop that closed its doors in 1998.

Save the Redwoods League bought that timberland in 2025 from the Mendocino Redwood Company, which had allowed Gianni’s members to build trails and ride their bikes on the property.

Through the years, the cycling association, an all-volunteer nonprofit, has been the beating heart of mountain biking in west Sonoma County, earning a reputation for its superb stewardship of the land and the high quality of its trails. The steep singletracks — narrow, natural surface paths — and fast flow sections are designed to maximize fun while minimizing impact on the environment.

Tom “Snap” Gonnella, who owned Gianni’s Cyclery and founded the club named after it, recalled in a recent podcast, “We were trying to be as inclusive as we could, but we had to deal with the landlord, who was limiting us on how many bikes that we could have in there.”

Now in the hands of Regional Parks, the cap on users is lifted. “We get to share it with everyone,” says Jake Bayless, a Gianni member who notes that, due to the park’s relative remoteness, fears of overcrowding have faded. “Everybody loves seeing more people riding bikes and smiling,” he says. “It’s a magic place.”

Learn more about becoming a volunteer member of the Gianni Cycling Association at giannicycling.org.

Riding the Redwoods

Most of the park’s trails fall in the intermediate category. An introductory route is the 2.3-mile Monte Rio Redwoods Trail, a lollipop loop through towering redwoods, along singletrack and old logging roads, featuring 600 feet of climbing, which even the fittest riders may find challenging.

A far more ambitious undertaking is the 6.8-mile Radar Love Loop, which calls for 1,765 feet of climbing and offers sweeping views of the Pacific Ocean at the halfway point.

Access trails via the park’s main entrance, 9610 Main St. in Monte Rio, or from the trailhead at 25572 Freezeout Road with a parking lot managed by California State Parks.

The Upper Willow Creek Road trailhead, offering access to a plethora of scenic routes — Badfinger, Sound of Music, Eastside and East Ramps loop, to name a few — has very limited parking along Willow Creek Road. Many bikers ride from Occidental, 5 miles away.

After riding the bikes-only Vacation Wonderland Trail at Monte Rio Redwoods, stop in at the newly opened Wonderland Pizzeria for a pie and a pint on their expansive patio. 20391 Highway 116, Monte Rio. 707-865-5133, instagram.com/wonderland_pizzeria

title: These Italian White Wines From Sonoma County Are Just Right for Summer
summary:
Italian white wine varieties are on the rise in Sonoma County — and the offerings go way beyond Pinot Grigio.

The post These Italian White Wines From Sonoma County Are Just Right for Summer appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
When it comes to crisp white wines, Sauvignon Blanc isn’t the only game in town. Italian white varieties are on the rise in Sonoma County — and the offerings go way beyond Pinot Grigio.

The delicious proof was on full display at this year’s North Coast Wine Challenge. Competing in the sweepstakes round for top honors were two Sonoma County Italians: a Fiano from DaVero Farms & Winery and a Biancolella d’Ischia from Orsi Family Vineyards.

The trend comes as no surprise to local winemakers like Sam Bilbro. He’s the founder and winemaker at Idlewild Wines in Healdsburg, which specializes in Italian-inspired wines.

“Italian varietals offer such a diversity of flavor profiles and joyful food friendliness,” says Bilbro, who makes wine from a Piedmontese grape called Erbaluce, planted at Las Cimas Ranch on the western edge of Russian River Valley.

“One of the qualities I love about this grape is that it has extreme fresh acidity matched with a textural mouthfeel,” he says. “I find that the aromatics are more driven by mineral tones and fresh Alpine scents with an undertone of orchard fruit.”

Eric Prahl, winemaker at Centennial Mountain Winery in Healdsburg, believes Sonoma County is an especially hospitable place for Italian whites. The Centennial Mountain vineyard includes California’s only planting of Carricante, hailing from Sicily.

“Italian varieties like Carricante have evolved over centuries to maintain balance in warm climates, which makes them highly relevant for the future of Sonoma County,” he says. “They offer a texture and a savory, saline quality that is still relatively uncommon here.”

Bilbro points out that Italian whites grown here sometimes express themselves a little differently in the glass.

“If made in a restrained style,” he says, “I find that Sonoma County is very true to the core of the varietals, as well as showing perhaps just a touch of California sunshine in the fruit tone.”

Three to try

Idlewild Wines

2023 Erbaluce, Las Cimas Vineyard, Russian River Valley, $42

With a vibrant golden color, Idlewild’s Erbaluce combines notes of lemon, fresh herbs and bright acidity. Made without oak, it’s fresh, juicy and food-friendly. 132 Plaza St., Healdsburg, 707-385-9410, idlewildwines.com

Orsi Family Vineyards

2024 Biancolella d’Ischia, Dry Creek Valley, $28

Made from a grape traditionally grown on the island of Ischia, Biancolella is known for its crispness, light body and subtle almond finish. Orsi’s is true to type — a mineral-kissed wine with tropical fruit aromas. 2306 Magnolia Drive, Healdsburg, 707-732-4660, orsifamilyvineyards.com

Centennial Mountain

2022 Carricante, Sonoma County , $49

With a lightly floral aroma, this energetic white shows off notes of citrus, minerals and fresh herbs. Intense, yet full of freshness and zing. It is delicious now, but you could also lay it down for a couple years to see how it develops. 337 Healdsburg Ave., Healdsburg, 669-240-5611, cmvineyard.com

title: Sonoma County Gas Stations Pumping Out Great Grub
summary:
Here are some Sonoma County gas stations with food options that may make the price at the pump a little easier to swallow.

The post Sonoma County Gas Stations Pumping Out Great Grub appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
It’s summertime, which means road trips and hungry travelers clamoring for quick eats. Sure, there are drive-ins, but there are some unexpected surprises at full service fuel shops where you can fill up your car and your belly. We’re not talking about sad hot dogs spinning on roller grills.

Here are some Sonoma County gas stations whose food options may make the price at the pump a little easier to swallow.

Wine Country Café & Deli

Stop in at the Fast Fill Market and Gulf station and treat yourself to the marvelous from-scratch scones, organic apple hand pies, all-day breakfast (smoked salmon croissant!) and plump, made-to-order sandwiches (legit banh mi and coffee-rubbed barbecue tri-tip). Spring through autumn finds barbecue, smashburgers, or street taco pop-ups every Friday in the parking lot. 5855 Sonoma Highway, Santa Rosa. 707-230-2462, winecountrycafedeli.toast.site

Husary 76

Its website lists it as a “convenience store,” but besides diesel and propane, you’ll discover gourmet grub such as real-deal Mexican hot chocolate, and — get this — a countertop wine fridge filled with olive oil crafted from a grove of trees nearby. Station owner and lifelong Sonoma County resident Mousa Husary looked to his Palestinian roots for planting his orchards and producing award-winning extra-virgin cold-pressed olive oil. 2110 Gravenstein Highway N., Sebastopol. 707-829-8252, husaryoliveoil.com

Bonneau Country

A gas station that has its own website with a category titled “cuisine”? This is Wine Country, after all. Find snacks and an early-morning drive-thru barista window at the station’s northern outpost at Arnold Drive and Grove Street. Five miles south at the roundabout, where Highway 116 meets Highway 121, the Carneros Deli just across the parking lot from the fueling and electric charging stations is the place for made-to-order delights: hot and cold sandwiches built from fancy stuff like premium prosciutto, provolone, all the fixings, and an array of breads and spreads including the must-have “spicy boom boom” sauce. 19080 Arnold Drive and 23001 Arnold Drive, Sonoma. 707-939-1646, bonneaucountry.com

Fuel & Food Market

The calling card is the Krispy Krunchy Chicken sign, beckoning you in for the cult-favorite hand-battered bird, the real discovery, though, is the under-the-radar Indian market filled with pantry staples like lentils, rice, and spices ranging from cardamom to black mustard seed. Even the frozen food is a step-up from ordinary, including naan, samosas and kulfi, an Indian specialty similar to ice cream. 4856 Old Redwood Highway, Santa Rosa. 707-843-4083

Vinoma Tapas Argentina

It’s not technically within a gas station, yet beckons from the adjacent Shell parking lot a few steps away. And you would be hard-pressed to find better fast-casual empanadas. These golden-brown Argentinian treats are stuffed with goodness like traditional spiced beef, a vegan curry tofu, or specialties like the plum, bacon, fontina and mozzarella open-faced version called canastita. 5085 Redwood Drive, Rohnert Park. 707-536-9215, vinoma.net

title: Inside Carrusel, Santa Rosa’s Over-The-Top Pink Bruncheria
summary:
Carrusel owner Ivy Reyes has transformed a childhood dream into an over-the-top Santa Rosa bruncheria filled with pink velvet, carousel horses and playful Mexi-brunch dishes.

The post Inside Carrusel, Santa Rosa’s Over-The-Top Pink Bruncheria appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Santa Rosa’s newest — and pinkest — brunch spot began with Ivy Reyes’ childhood dream of owning an Easy-Bake Oven.

Though her family couldn’t afford one, Reyes never forgot the toy oven or her dream of opening a bakery. Decades later, she opened Carrusel, a portal to her youth and a fantasyland of glitter, bows, flowers and carousel horses that makes Barbie’s Dreamhouse look restrained.

“My childhood is poured into here,” Reyes said.

Dressed head to toe in sparkles and sipping a pink Red Bull at 11 a.m. on a Wednesday (what else would she drink?), Reyes radiates Barbie glamour. At 33, the Instagram influencer, who drives a pink Range Rover and dreams up elaborate social media promotions, is very much queen of all she surveys.

“This is just me,” she said, wrapping manicured pink nails around the heart-shaped straw in her energy drink. “I put it together for the love of food, color and a dream. I want it to be an enchantment.”

These days, Reyes is no longer dreaming about an Easy-Bake Oven. She’s overseeing a staff of 50, an ambitious cocktail program and a six-page Mexi-brunch menu that keeps the kitchen busy.

Family roots

Beneath the spectacle is a family story built on work and sacrifice.

Reyes, her immigrant parents and two brothers shared a one-bedroom apartment while the family built La Fondita restaurant and Elenita’s food truck in Roseland. She grew up alongside her mother in the kitchen, learning both the food and business sides of the restaurant industry.

“Growing up, it was very, very worrisome when my parents were starting out and living check to check,” she said. “I remember that, and it keeps me humble.”

Her mother eventually gave Reyes the opportunity to build something of her own, transforming the former La Fondita downtown into something entirely new.

“She put everything on a silver platter,” Reyes said. “From there, she said, ‘Fly with it. You’re on your own.’”

Reyes had hoped her grandmother would be the first person through Carrusel’s doors. Before she died, Reyes showed her the nearly finished restaurant by phone from the hospital and received her blessing.

“I’ve had people of all ages tear up here,” Reyes said. “It brings out the inner child in everyone.”

Flowers, candles and bright colors had always lifted her spirits, and she wanted Carrusel to offer guests the same escape.

“When your world goes gray, paint it pink,” she said. “You can have a bad day, come in here and forget the problems you’re having.”

Best bets

Carrusel is about fun and fantasy rather than fine dining. Expect cotton-candy-topped cocktails, tacos served on a high wire and a Mexi-brunch menu that blends American and Latin flavors with carnival flair. Desserts lean unapologetically sweet, with glazes, marshmallows and chocolate piled high.

And yes, you can eat on the outdoor carousel, which somehow makes everything taste more fun.

Raspberry Mocha Truffle, $8: The fact that I’ve ordered this three times says plenty about my weakness for sugar, glitter and caffeine. Thick raspberry foam (banana and blueberry are also available), edible butterflies (I use “edible” loosely) and chocolatey iced mocha make this a memorable way to start the day. Or night.

Queso Birria Tacos, $20: One of the menu’s most entertaining presentations, with three consommé-soaked birria tacos suspended on a clothesline-like rack. Fiery avocado salsa and extra consommé for dipping complete the show.

Enmoladas, $20: Not the prettiest dish on the menu, but one of the most satisfying. Rich, dark mole blankets chicken-filled tortillas. Sometimes no glitter is needed.

Brunch Board, $35: Order this butterfly-shaped board simply because you can. It comes loaded with banana French toast, strawberry-topped pancakes, a berry-topped Belgian waffle, fresh fruit and Nutella.

Funnel Cake, $18: This fairground favorite is available year-round, piled high with fruit, powdered sugar, chocolate and bananas whenever the craving strikes.

Japanese Pancakes, $18: These take about 20 minutes to make and involve a special technique known only to the kitchen. They aren’t quite as airy as the versions popularized in Japan, but they’re close enough.

Cloud Nine, $18: Dragon berry rum, lychee, lemon and vanilla topped with a cloud of cotton candy — exactly what your 9-year-old self imagined you would be drinking at 21.

Mimosa Flight, $38: Every mimosa should come this way. More brunchy fun for everyone.

Chilaquiles, $19: Judging by the number landing on neighboring tables, this may be the restaurant’s most popular dish.

Open from 7 a.m. to 10 p.m. daily. Carrusel is at 630 Third St., Santa Rosa, 707-655-8365, instagram.com/cafe_carrusel.

title: Saucy Mama’s Jook Joint in Guerneville is the Spot People Plan Vacations Around
summary:
Yvette Bidegain carries on her father’s barbecue legacy with catfish, ribs, fried chicken and plenty of personality at Saucy Mama’s Jook Joint.

The post Saucy Mama’s Jook Joint in Guerneville is the Spot People Plan Vacations Around appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Yvette Bidegain thought she knew what Californians wanted to eat. Okra and catfish weren’t on the list.

Four years after opening Saucy Mama’s Jook Joint in Guerneville, they’re her two best-selling dishes.

“I used to sneak catfish to my friends’ table because they really wanted it,” she said. Other diners noticed and started asking for it, too. Eventually, the farm-raised catfish earned a permanent place on the menu.

Saucy Mama’s is equal parts soul food restaurant, neighborhood hangout, birthday destination and post-river stop, wrapped in a barbecue-roadhouse-meets-New Orleans aesthetic.

Tucked along a bend in Highway 116 west of downtown Guerneville, it’s the kind of place many drivers pass on their way to the coast. Yet Saucy Mama’s is almost always full, with Bidegain greeting guests and keeping the dining room humming. Some regulars even plan vacations around getting a “Saucy Mama fix.”

Bidegain’s menu blends the Southern cooking of her family’s Louisiana and Mississippi roots with her own California sensibility. Since opening in 2022, the restaurant has built a loyal following.

The backstory

Bidegain is the daughter of Leroy Richardson, whose Richardson’s Ribs was a Sonoma County Fair favorite in the 1980s and ’90s before expanding into restaurants in Santa Rosa and Sebastopol. His recipes remain the backbone of Saucy Mama’s menu.

At first, Bidegain resisted leaning on the family name.

“I didn’t want to take my dad’s name down with me,” she said.

Then her mother tasted Bidegain’s gumbo and delivered the compliment that mattered most: “Baby, your gumbo tastes just like your daddy’s.”

She knew she was onto something.

Richardson’s recipes live on in Bidegain’s kitchen, while signs, menus, family photographs and other mementos from his restaurants cover the walls.

Not every dish would have earned her father’s approval. Bidegain jokes he’s probably rolling over in his grave over the tofu po’ boy and meatless succotash.

Even the restaurant’s bright red smoker felt like fate. Bidegain had gone to a restaurant supply store looking for a sink and instead found a used Texas smoker she’d long pined for — marked down to half price.

“A lot of things happened like that for us,” she said. “I truly think my father was orchestrating it from heaven.”

Here’s what to know before you go.

Yvette’s favorite dish

Pork ribs.

Fun fact

Bidegain didn’t like soul food growing up. While her friends ate spaghetti with Parmesan, she dreaded collard greens, neck bones and black-eyed peas.

That changed in her 20s, when she started cooking for herself. During her pregnancy, she found herself craving the dishes she’d once avoided.

“It’s just in my DNA,” she said. “Your blood takes over.”

The vibe

You will not get in without a reservation, so don’t try to sweet-talk Bidegain, who is usually at the front door greeting guests. When the restaurant is full, it’s full.

The crowd ranges from birthday celebrants in dress clothes to river-goers in flip-flops, and nobody looks out of place.

Inside, Saucy Mama’s is a joyful jumble of vintage New Orleans signs, memorabilia from Richardson’s restaurants, Black art and hundreds of donated knickknacks. Maximalist hardly begins to describe it.

Every holiday brings another round of decorations. “Restraint” is not in her vocabulary. Bidegain originally envisioned a true jook joint with live music and dancing, but the restaurant became so popular there’s barely room between the tables.

The food

Come hungry. Portions are generous, and nobody comes here to count calories.

Crispy fried catfish entree, $20: The seasoned cornmeal crust is crisp and flavorful, without the heavy, bready coating that can sink lesser catfish. Inside, the farm-raised fish is moist, succulent and clean-tasting.

Shrimp po’ boy, $22: A small French loaf is cut into a boat rather than sliced through, holding a messy pile of fried shrimp, lettuce, tomatoes and remoulade.

Buttermilk fried chicken entree, $25: The boldly seasoned crust fries up crisp, giving way to juicy meat. Pair it with red beans and rice and collard greens for the soul food holy trinity. The loose bits of crunchy crust left on the plate are worth chasing with a fork. Served with cornbread waffles, crack butter and two sides.

Barbecue pork ribs entree, $28: Coated in Bidegain’s secret dry rub for at least 24 hours before spending hours in the smoker, the ribs are deeply smoky and tender. They’re slathered in a sweet barbecue sauce and best eaten with plenty of napkins. Served with cornbread waffles, crack butter and two sides.

Extras, $8: Great barbecue restaurants live or die by their sides. Here, the macaroni and cheese — made with four cheeses and cream — is rich and satisfying. The standout, though, is the fried okra tossed with onions and bacon.

All meats are available à la carte, including a full rack of pork ribs and fried chicken.

Banana pudding, $6: Even banana pudding skeptics may be won over by this version, layered into a shortbread crust and topped with whipped cream.

The menu also includes several gluten-free and vegetarian options, along with beer, cider, wine and nonalcoholic drinks.

The discount

Because Bidegain spent years as a Caltrans equipment operator, she offers a 10% discount to fellow operating engineers.

The spot

16632 Highway 116, Guerneville, 707-604-7184, saucymamasjookjoint.com

title: Bay Area Designer’s Cape Dutch-Style Home Hits the Market in Glen Ellen
summary:
The Glen Ellen home references traditional architecture from South Africa’s acclaimed wine region and includes whimsical touches like cast-iron street lamps and a British phone booth.

The post Bay Area Designer’s Cape Dutch-Style Home Hits the Market in Glen Ellen appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
A Glen Ellen home with Cape Dutch style is currently listed for sale. The farmhouse, guest house, barn-style office and pool on 16 acres is currently seeking $12,000,000.

The home is the work of resident and designer Patrick Printy — a veteran style-maker for major brands, such as Levi’s and Restoration Hardware, and lead of his own firm with projects published in magazines from Elle Decor to House Beautiful. 

This particular three-bedroom, three-bathroom farmhouse references traditional architecture from South Africa’s wine country. A unique design for the Sonoma area, the dwelling has the signature Cape Dutch scalloped, ornamented gables. Inside, there’s handcrafted Dutch cabinetry by Johannes Van Mourik and also handmade Dutch “witjes” tiles.

Use of grandly sized oak wood beams and floor planks, reclaimed from Midwestern barns, creates dramatic farm character throughout. The property’s exterior stonework was sourced from rocks quarried from the property.

Eclectic textiles create a cohesive but collected look. The interiors are an impossibly successful mix of old and new, clean-lined and traditional with pleasing dollops of fun tossed in. This is exemplified right at the front door where black-and-white traditional symmetry is made playful with the addition of wonderfully “matchy” Dalmatian statues. Vintage cast-iron street lamps, sourced from San Francisco’s China Basin, and a British phone booth offer spectacular whimsy to the grounds.

The grounds include a pond, a well and solar panels. There are two additional parcels for future development.

title: Sebastopol’s Famous Monte-Bellaria Estate and Lavender Farm for Sale
summary:
Boasting over 38,000 lavender plants, Monte-Bellaria has long drawn visitors with its rich sensory experience and handmade lavender products. Now the farm and hilltop home is on the market.

The post Sebastopol’s Famous Monte-Bellaria Estate and Lavender Farm for Sale appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
A Sebastopol estate with a lavender farm — one of the largest in northern California — is currently listed for sale. A four-bedroom, three-and-half-bathroom home on 14 acres with 38,000 lavender plants, an olive orchard, apiary and farm store are listed for $4,995,000.

The property, named Monte-Bellaria — meaning “mountain of beautiful air” in Italian — has been a beloved stop along the Sonoma County Farm Trails. The land, stewarded since 2002 by the late Dr. Bill MacElroy, has sloping rows of the hardy and fragrant Grosso lavender plant.

Yearly, MacElroy, along with farm manager and beekeeper Eric Silas, cultivated and harvested the lavender, from which he would distill the essential oils to create the property’s popular products: soaps, balms, hydrosols and a sumptuous lavender honey. The handmade goods, including olive oils made from the yields of their orchard, were sold at the on-site farm store. Monte-Bellaria became a popular site for visitors seeking tranquility, a bit of shopping and a swoon-worthy photo backdrop.

A walk through the grounds is a rich sensory experience. In addition to the immense fragrance during high bloom season, there’s a sound bath of buzzing from the bees hard at work pollinating the plants. 

The 4,965-square-foot hilltop home, built in 2014, takes style cues from the Tuscan countryside, which inspired MacElroy’s development of the farm. The dwelling is airy with high ceilings, lime-washed walls in earth tones, walnut-stained millwork and natural stone. Plentiful windows offer sweeping views of lavender and neighboring vineyards.

Amenities include an additional prep kitchen, an elevator and an outdoor brick oven. A secondary unit is a tranquil spot with the same luxury finishes.

For more information on Monte-Bellaria at 3518 Bloomfield Road in Sebastopol, contact listing agents Mallory Lambert Silipo, 707-478-5342, Pamela Ranella, 707-810-5066; Home Girls of Sonoma County, 130 Petaluma Ave., Suite 1-C, Sebastopol, 3518bloomfieldroad.com

content:
Bali Wedding Catering Food Ideas to Impress Guests

 

Choosing the right wedding catering makes a huge difference to the success of the wedding. Bali’s incredible produce, international culinary talent, and tropical setting provide endless opportunities to create a menu that reflects both your personality and the destination.

Planning a wedding in Bali is about creating an unforgettable experience, and few things leave a bigger impression than exceptional food. Guests may forget the colour of the flowers or the style of the chairs, but they will always remember a meal that was beautifully presented, full of flavour, and thoughtfully planned.

Here are some of the best Bali wedding catering food ideas that will leave your guests talking long after the celebration ends.

Work with an Experienced Bali Wedding Caterer

Experienced catering teams coordinate closely with wedding planners, venues and suppliers to ensure every course is served on time and to the highest standard.

From menu planning and tastings through to logistics, staffing and dietary requirements, professional caterers help ensure your wedding runs seamlessly from beginning to end.

Whether you envision an elegant plated dinner, an extravagant buffet, interactive live cooking stations, or a combination of dining styles, working with an experienced Bali wedding caterer such as Bali Catering and Events, allows you to create a menu that reflects your personalities while delivering an unforgettable experience for every guest.

 

Welcome Guests with Elegant Canapés

Bali is hot and humid, and people want light food and refreshing drinks. The cocktail hour sets the tone for the rest of the evening. Rather than having guests wait for the main meal, welcome them with beautifully presented canapés served alongside champagne or your own personalised signature cocktails.

Popular canapé ideas include:

  • Seared scallops with zesty citrus sauce
  • Mini wagyu beef sliders
  • Caviar blinis
  • Fresh tuna tartare
  • Mushroom arancini
  • Duck pancakes
  • Tempura prawns
  • Caprese skewers
  • Goat’s cheese and beetroot crostini
  • Mini lobster rolls

A mix of seafood, meat and vegetarian options ensures there is something for everyone while encouraging guests to mingle before dinner.

Create Interactive Live Food Stations

Live cooking stations are becoming one of the biggest trends in luxury Bali weddings. They combine incredible food with entertainment, allowing chefs to prepare dishes fresh in front of guests.

Some of the most popular stations include:

Taco Station

Tacos served to guests in a convenience and interactive way. 

Seafood Bar

Fresh oysters, prawns, lobster, crab and sashimi displayed on ice create an eye-catching centrepiece while showcasing the freshest local seafood.

BBQ Grill

Premium steaks, seafood, chicken and vegetables are grilled live, filling the venue with irresistible aromas.

Satay Grill

A Balinese favourite where chefs prepare chicken, beef and seafood satay over charcoal, served with traditional sauces.

Sushi Station

Fresh sushi and sashimi prepared throughout the evening adds theatre while offering lighter dining options.

Interactive stations encourage guests to explore different flavours while creating a more relaxed and social dining experience.

Offer a Premium Grazing Table

A luxury grazing table has become a wedding favourite for good reason. Beautifully styled with artisan ingredients, it immediately captures attention while giving guests something to enjoy throughout cocktail hour.

A premium grazing table may include:

  • Imported cheeses
  • Artisan cured meats
  • Fresh tropical fruits
  • Seasonal berries
  • Gourmet crackers
  • Fresh breads
  • House-made dips
  • Marinated olives
  • Nuts
  • Honeycomb
  • Dried fruits
  • Smoked salmon
  • Fresh figs
  • Chocolate treats

Not only does it look stunning, but it also caters to a wide variety of tastes and dietary preferences.

 

Choose a Family Style Dining Experience

Family-style dining has become increasingly popular for destination weddings because it creates a warm and social atmosphere.

Instead of individually plated meals, beautifully presented sharing platters are placed in the centre of each table, encouraging guests to pass dishes around and enjoy the meal together.

Popular sharing dishes include:

  • Slow roasted lamb shoulder
  • Whole roasted beef tenderloin
  • Chargrilled seafood platters
  • Roast chicken with herbs
  • Mediterranean vegetables
  • Gourmet salads
  • Garlic potatoes
  • Grilled seasonal vegetables
  • Fresh artisan breads

This style of dining often feels more relaxed while still maintaining a premium experience.

 

Include Local Balinese Flavours

Many couples choose Bali because they want guests to experience the destination. Including authentic Balinese and Indonesian dishes alongside international favourites allows visitors to enjoy local flavours without making the entire menu unfamiliar.

Some excellent additions include:

  • Chicken satay
  • Beef rendang
  • Nasi goreng
  • Mie goreng
  • Babi guling
  • Lawar
  • Pepes ikan
  • Balinese grilled seafood
  • Sambal selections
  • Fresh tropical salads

Combining Balinese cuisine with international dishes gives guests the best of both worlds.

 

Impress with Premium Seafood

Being surrounded by the ocean means Bali offers access to exceptional seafood that is perfect for weddings.

Premium seafood options include:

  • Fresh lobster
  • King prawns
  • Oysters
  • Yellowfin tuna
  • Barramundi
  • Snapper
  • Salmon
  • Scallops
  • Crab
  • Octopus

Add a Late Night Supper

Presentation Matters as Much as the Food

Conclusion

Your wedding menu is one of the most memorable parts of your celebration. By combining premium ingredients, creative presentation, interactive food experiences and exceptional service, you can create a dining experience that your guests will remember long after they return home.

From luxurious seafood bars and elegant canapé receptions to family-style feasts, gourmet grazing tables and live cooking stations, Bali offers endless opportunities to impress your guests with incredible food. With thoughtful planning and an experienced catering team, your wedding catering can become one of the true highlights of your special day.

content:
Luxury in Indonesia is evolving. While premium travel, fine dining, and exclusive experiences remain highly sought after, one culinary delicacy is becoming increasingly desirable among discerning consumers: caviar. Once considered a product reserved for European royalty and Michelin-starred restaurants, caviar is now finding its place in Indonesia’s luxury dining scene, private celebrations, luxury villas, superyachts, and high-end hospitality venues.

As more Indonesians and international visitors embrace gourmet food experiences, caviar has become a symbol of sophistication, exclusivity, and refined taste. Whether enjoyed during an intimate dinner overlooking the ocean in Bali, paired with Champagne at a luxury event in Jakarta, or served as part of a private chef experience on board a yacht in Komodo, caviar is quickly becoming one of Indonesia’s most sought-after luxury foods.

Why Caviar Is Growing in Popularity

Today’s luxury consumer is looking beyond traditional status symbols. Rather than simply purchasing luxury goods, many people are investing in memorable experiences, exceptional food, and exclusive dining moments. Caviar perfectly represents this shift.

Its rarity, meticulous production process, and distinctive flavour make it unlike any other ingredient. Every serving tells a story of craftsmanship, patience, and quality. As appreciation for fine food continues to grow throughout Indonesia, more people are discovering why caviar has been regarded as one of the world’s finest delicacies for centuries.

International tourism has also played a major role. Indonesia welcomes visitors from around the world who are already familiar with premium caviar and expect the same level of luxury during their stay. Hotels, restaurants, beach clubs, and private dining venues are increasingly adding caviar to their menus to meet these expectations while creating memorable culinary experiences.

 

Choosing Quality Matters

As interest in caviar continues to increase, choosing a trusted supplier has become more important than ever.

Authentic premium caviar should be carefully sourced, professionally stored, and transported under strict temperature-controlled conditions to preserve its freshness, texture, and flavour.

Working with an experienced supplier such as Caviar Indonesia, ensures customers receive genuine, high-quality caviar that reflects the standards expected from one of the world’s most prestigious delicacies.

Whether purchasing for a fine dining restaurant, luxury hotel, private event, or personal enjoyment, quality and freshness should always remain the highest priorities.

Luxury Dining Is Changing

Indonesia’s fine dining scene has matured significantly over the past decade. Cities such as Jakarta, Bali, and Surabaya are now home to award-winning restaurants, internationally trained chefs, luxury resorts, and premium hospitality experiences that rival those found anywhere in the world.

Chefs are using caviar not simply as an extravagant garnish but as an ingredient that enhances carefully crafted dishes. Small amounts of premium caviar can elevate seafood, oysters, handmade pasta, wagyu beef, Japanese cuisine, blinis, potato dishes, and even modern desserts.

The delicate saltiness and complex flavour profile provide a luxurious finish that cannot easily be replicated by any other ingredient. This ability to transform a dish has made caviar one of the most desirable additions to contemporary fine dining menus.

 

The Rise of Private Luxury Experiences

One of the biggest trends in Indonesia is the growing demand for personalised luxury experiences.

Private chefs, exclusive villa dining, intimate celebrations, yacht charters, and bespoke events have become increasingly popular among travellers and local residents alike. Rather than visiting crowded restaurants, many guests now prefer having world-class dining brought directly to them.

Caviar naturally complements these premium experiences.

Imagine watching the sunset from a private villa in Bali while enjoying freshly shucked oysters topped with premium caviar, or celebrating a special occasion aboard a luxury yacht with Champagne and carefully selected caviar served by a private chef. These exclusive moments are exactly what modern luxury consumers are seeking.

As demand for these personalised experiences continues to grow, so too does the demand for premium caviar throughout Indonesia.

 

More Than Just Fine Dining

Although caviar is closely associated with luxury restaurants, its appeal extends far beyond traditional dining establishments.

Today, premium caviar is frequently enjoyed during:

  • Private celebrations
  • Luxury weddings
  • Corporate entertaining
  • VIP events
  • Yacht charters
  • Villa dining experiences
  • Five-star hotel experiences
  • Champagne tastings
  • Exclusive product launches
  • Luxury gifting

Its elegant presentation immediately enhances any occasion, making guests feel they are experiencing something truly special.

For event planners and luxury hospitality providers, caviar has become an effective way to create memorable experiences that guests continue talking about long after the event has finished.

 

Pairing Caviar with Premium Beverages

One reason caviar has become increasingly fashionable is its versatility when paired with premium beverages.

Champagne remains the classic accompaniment, with its crisp acidity balancing the rich, buttery texture of caviar. However, premium sparkling wines, chilled vodka, sake, fine white wines, and even carefully selected cocktails can also create exceptional pairings.

Many luxury venues now offer curated food and beverage pairings that allow guests to experience how different drinks complement various caviar varieties.

These tasting experiences have become increasingly popular among food enthusiasts looking to expand their culinary knowledge while enjoying one of the world’s most prestigious delicacies.

 

An Ingredient That Represents Exclusivity

Unlike many luxury foods, caviar cannot be mass produced quickly.

Sturgeon require many years before they begin producing roe, making genuine caviar naturally limited in supply. This lengthy production process contributes to its exclusivity and reinforces its position as one of the world’s most luxurious ingredients.

For consumers, serving authentic caviar represents an appreciation for quality, craftsmanship, and exceptional culinary experiences.

Whether entertaining business clients or celebrating life’s biggest milestones, caviar has become a statement of refined taste rather than simply a luxury purchase.

The Growing Demand Across Indonesia

While Bali has become one of Indonesia’s leading destinations for luxury dining, demand for premium caviar is growing throughout the country.

Restaurants, luxury hotels, private clubs, and hospitality venues across Jakarta, Surabaya, Bandung, Lombok, and other major destinations are increasingly incorporating caviar into their culinary offerings.

Private customers are also purchasing caviar to enjoy at home, creating restaurant-quality experiences without leaving their own dining rooms.

As access to premium imported products continues to improve, authentic caviar has become more accessible than ever for consumers seeking exceptional gourmet experiences.

 

Caviar Indonesia Leading the Luxury Movement

As appreciation for gourmet cuisine continues to grow, Caviar Indonesia is helping shape the country’s evolving luxury food culture by supplying premium imported caviar to restaurants, hotels, chefs, event organisers, businesses, and private customers across Indonesia.

With an extensive selection of carefully sourced caviar varieties, professional handling, and reliable nationwide delivery, Caviar Indonesia makes it easier than ever to enjoy authentic premium caviar for every occasion.

From intimate dinners and luxury weddings to five-star hospitality, corporate entertaining, and unforgettable celebrations, Caviar Indonesia provides the products that transform exceptional dining into truly memorable experiences.

 

Conclusion

Luxury is no longer defined solely by expensive possessions. Increasingly, it is measured by unique experiences, unforgettable moments, and exceptional food shared with family, friends, and colleagues.

Caviar perfectly embodies this new definition of luxury. It combines heritage, craftsmanship, rarity, and extraordinary flavour into an ingredient that instantly elevates any occasion.

As Indonesia’s hospitality industry continues to grow and consumers become more adventurous in their culinary choices, premium caviar is expected to play an even greater role in fine dining and luxury entertaining.

What was once considered a rare indulgence is now becoming one of the defining ingredients of Indonesia’s modern luxury lifestyle. For those seeking the very best in gourmet experiences, Caviar Indonesia is leading the way by bringing the world’s finest caviar to tables across the archipelago.

title: Local Chef’s ‘Hell Chicken’ Might Be a Taste of Heaven on Earth
summary:
How does chef Lee Desrosiers make his New York Times-recognized "Hell Chicken" so mind-blowingly delicious? The devil, as the saying goes, is in the details.

The post Local Chef’s ‘Hell Chicken’ Might Be a Taste of Heaven on Earth appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Deep in the redwoods of west county, almond and oak smoke curls around the field kitchen chef Lee Desrosiers has parked at the end of his gravel driveway. The converted pig smoker is an amalgamation of grates, pipes, bricks, meat hooks, cast iron, and steel welded into a Frankencooker built for one very specific purpose: making his signature Hell Chicken.

Named for pollo alla diavola, the Italian name for an aggressively seasoned, spatchcocked chicken cooked over screaming-high heat, the title is more joke than homage—though the chickens might disagree.

Above hellfire-hot embers, whole birds hang from curved metal hooks, roasting slowly in a process powered by little more than salt, smoke, heat, and time. Desrosiers has spent more than a decade perfecting it, first on the East Coast and now in Sonoma County, where he’s made his home. What began as a weekend lark on a Brooklyn sidewalk has become a mission for the 42-year-old chef.

As fat renders and smoke drifts into the trees, Desrosiers works mostly by instinct, checking the coals and watching for the moment the skin tightens against the meat. Timing matters, but feel matters more.

His black Lab-Pit Bull mix, Frankie, knows the routine, circling the grill in hopes that gravity and good fortune might deliver an errant scrap, until a rustle in the tall grass sends her trotting into the weeds. Priorities.

She knows by smell that the chicken is nearly ready. What she doesn’t know is that I’m about to lose all objectivity over what may be the best chicken I’ll ever eat.

Brooklyn was where Desrosiers’ obsession with live-fire cooking first took shape. Already an accomplished chef, he landed there just as the borough’s artisanal food scene was exploding, fueled by the farm-to-table ethos of restaurants like Blue Hill, Superfine, and Marlow & Sons. He haunted farmers markets, learned to break down whole animals, and cooked in the stripped-down, ingredient-driven style that redefined dining from Austin to the Bay Area.

He spent a year working as a butcher at Achilles Heel, the Greenpoint gastropub where he’d eventually launch Hell Chicken, which gave him an intimate understanding of how muscle, fat, and connective tissue behave over heat, whether braised, grilled, or smoked.

On weekends, he would drag a grill into an empty parking space, first cooking chickens directly over hot coals before gradually jerry-rigging a setup that could smoke and braise them, too. Served half or whole with a simple salad, the dish felt ridiculously uncomplicated.

He kept refining the rig and fine tuning the bird, then in October 2016, The New York Times took notice. Suddenly, Desrosiers had an overnight poultry phenomenon on his hands.

“You are given forks and knives, but it’s hard to resist pulling off morsels of the golden skin with your fingers as if you were standing around in the kitchen at home,” critic Oliver Strand wrote. Within days, Desrosiers could barely cook fast enough to feed the crowds.

But California soon came calling. In 2018, he traded coasts after Scribe Winery offered him a job on its culinary team. Northern California wasn’t entirely new territory, however, and in some ways, it felt like a return.

“I happened upon Northern California on a post-college journey west, equal parts Kerouac and Bob Dylan, searching for some kind of gold, I guess,” says Desrosiers. “Half adventure, half accident, like so many Californians before me. Sonoma County has been that golden place for me.”

It was Sebastopol that won him over: a funky, rural pocket filled with orchards, towering redwoods, ocean air, and the kind of wide-open spaces a cramped Brooklyn parking spot could never offer. Having San Francisco’s eclectic restaurant scene just down the road didn’t hurt either.

The move gave Desrosiers room to evolve beyond the constraints of restaurant kitchens and parking space grilling. These days, he’s focused almost entirely on private events and live-fire cooking experiences, though he hints there may be more pop-ups in other cities ahead. His summer calendar is packed with birthdays, weddings, private dinners, and ticketed events across Sonoma County. At a single event, he may cook anywhere from a few dozen to more than 100 birds over a showstopper of a rig that resembles a Ferris wheel: Two towering 5-foot rings are connected by crossbars, enabling him to suspend chickens over an open fire pit like some kind of poultry carnival ride.

“It invites people into the cooking process,” he says. “The visual aspect of the whole thing is arresting and enchanting. Cooking usually happens behind closed doors. This provides connection.”

When it comes to what makes Desrosiers’ Hell Chicken so mind-blowingly delicious, the devil, as the saying goes, is in the details. He starts with Mary’s organic chicken, specifically the Freedom Ranger, a slower-growing bird than typical commercial broilers that are bred for oversized breasts and harvested at six-to-eight weeks. These birds have more balanced bodies and get nine-to-12 weeks to develop a fuller flavor, which Desrosiers says makes them especially suited to live-fire cooking.

The night before cooking, he dry rubs each bird—no secret seasonings— just salt, which results in juicy, deeply seasoned meat with extra-crispy skin. The next day, he hangs the chickens over embers until the skin tightens—usually 90 minutes to two hours—then transfers them to a Dutch oven banked with coals to braise in their own jus before moving them back to the grill to get crackling skin. It’s served with a squeeze of lemon and a pour of the concentrated braising juices, a sort of liquid gold that should probably be bottled and sold.

It all seems so utterly simple. Those hours of labor seem to evaporate the minute the meat hits the plate. Which is part of the point.

The drive to Desrosiers’ place is its own adventure, complete with GPS wrong turns, dirt roads, and wildlife darting through the brush. By the time I pull up, the smoke still perfumes the air. He’s set aside a private meal for us on the patio, beneath trees rustling in the afternoon wind. A still-warm chicken waits in a Dutch oven. Desrosiers hands me a spoon and gestures toward the jus beneath the bird, a glossy puddle of rendered fat and juices. It’s salty, concentrated, and oh-so-easy to eat straight from the pot.

A skillet of rice cooked in schmaltz arrives brown and crunchy at the edges, alongside charred cabbage with butter beans dressed in sauce made with green chile and preserved lemon that lands somewhere between pesto and chimichurri, but with more swagger than either. Slices of chicken, skin still glistening, come with broth to ladle over the top.

Flavors unfold gently with each bite: salt, umami, buttery skin, a flicker of char, a quiet note of smoke in the background. This is what chicken should taste like in a perfect world. And right now, that world feels pretty close.

Sitting at the table with Desrosiers has its own quiet magic. He’s humble and generous giving advice for his method, while knowing this is a meal mere mortals could never quite pull off at home. Somehow it feels deeply familiar, the kind of food that nudges at memories you’re not even sure belong to you. Frankie circles the table, tail wagging, still hoping for a bite. I’m happy to oblige, because some meals are better shared.

Hell Chicken might not be in every cook’s wheelhouse, but Lee Desrosiers’ recipe for grilled cabbage is an ideal, carefree side dish for grilling nights. It will pair well with most any protein you feel like making.

Grilled Cabbage with Preserved Lime and Chile

Makes 4 servings

  • 1 head of cabbage, see note
  • 1 tbsp. avocado oil
  • Kosher salt
For the sauce:
  • 2 serrano chiles, seeded and diced
  • 1/2 preserved lime (lemon also works well), rinsed and seeds removed
  • 1 tbsp. Colatura (anchovy sauce, or substitute fish sauce)
  • Juice of 2 limes (or lemons)
  • 1 tsp. white wine vinegar
  • 3 tbsp. olive oil

Cut the cabbage into quarters and set aside.

While grill heats, make the sauce.

In a food processor combine chiles, preserved lime, anchovy sauce, lime juice, and vinegar. Pulse a few times, and then with the motor running, drizzle in the olive oil until the mixture emulsifies. Alternatively, you can make the sauce in a bowl by finely dicing the chiles and preserved lime, then whisking in the remaining ingredients. Set sauce aside until it’s time to serve.

Meanwhile, toss the cabbage with the avocado oil and season with a healthy pinch of salt. Place cabbage cut side down on the grill, and grill over hot coals, or if using propane, over medium-high heat. Sear until the cabbage begins to caramelize and soften. Remove cabbage to a serving platter and spoon the sauce over it. Serve at once with your favorite grilled protein.

Note: Plan on 1/4 of a cabbage per person. The type of cabbage you use also determines how you should cook it. If using a tight head of cabbage, such as common red or green grocery store varieties, blanch the cabbage quarters in a pot of boiling water first. Remove from the pot, pat dry, and continue with the recipe. Loose-leaf cabbages like Savoy or the cone-shaped Caraflex can go straight on the grill.

title: Monte Rio Redwoods Park Expands for Mountain Biking Recreation
summary:
A rugged Monte Rio refuge quadrupled in size last year, offering nearly 30 miles of trails lovingly maintained by an all-volunteer local cycling association.

The post Monte Rio Redwoods Park Expands for Mountain Biking Recreation appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
If you favor fat-tire biking and seek epic singletrack through postcard stands of Sequoia, head for Monte Rio Redwoods Park and Open Space Preserve. That rugged west county refuge quadrupled in size a year ago when Sonoma County Regional Parks acquired, from Save the Redwoods League, a 1,517-acre parcel laced with nearly 30 miles of trails. It was built and maintained for decades by members of the Gianni Cycling Association, named for the beloved Occidental bike shop that closed its doors in 1998.

Save the Redwoods League bought that timberland in 2025 from the Mendocino Redwood Company, which had allowed Gianni’s members to build trails and ride their bikes on the property.

Through the years, the cycling association, an all-volunteer nonprofit, has been the beating heart of mountain biking in west Sonoma County, earning a reputation for its superb stewardship of the land and the high quality of its trails. The steep singletracks — narrow, natural surface paths — and fast flow sections are designed to maximize fun while minimizing impact on the environment.

Tom “Snap” Gonnella, who owned Gianni’s Cyclery and founded the club named after it, recalled in a recent podcast, “We were trying to be as inclusive as we could, but we had to deal with the landlord, who was limiting us on how many bikes that we could have in there.”

Now in the hands of Regional Parks, the cap on users is lifted. “We get to share it with everyone,” says Jake Bayless, a Gianni member who notes that, due to the park’s relative remoteness, fears of overcrowding have faded. “Everybody loves seeing more people riding bikes and smiling,” he says. “It’s a magic place.”

Learn more about becoming a volunteer member of the Gianni Cycling Association at giannicycling.org.

Riding the Redwoods

Most of the park’s trails fall in the intermediate category. An introductory route is the 2.3-mile Monte Rio Redwoods Trail, a lollipop loop through towering redwoods, along singletrack and old logging roads, featuring 600 feet of climbing, which even the fittest riders may find challenging.

A far more ambitious undertaking is the 6.8-mile Radar Love Loop, which calls for 1,765 feet of climbing and offers sweeping views of the Pacific Ocean at the halfway point.

Access trails via the park’s main entrance, 9610 Main St. in Monte Rio, or from the trailhead at 25572 Freezeout Road with a parking lot managed by California State Parks.

The Upper Willow Creek Road trailhead, offering access to a plethora of scenic routes — Badfinger, Sound of Music, Eastside and East Ramps loop, to name a few — has very limited parking along Willow Creek Road. Many bikers ride from Occidental, 5 miles away.

After riding the bikes-only Vacation Wonderland Trail at Monte Rio Redwoods, stop in at the newly opened Wonderland Pizzeria for a pie and a pint on their expansive patio. 20391 Highway 116, Monte Rio. 707-865-5133, instagram.com/wonderland_pizzeria

title: These Italian White Wines From Sonoma County Are Just Right for Summer
summary:
Italian white wine varieties are on the rise in Sonoma County — and the offerings go way beyond Pinot Grigio.

The post These Italian White Wines From Sonoma County Are Just Right for Summer appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
When it comes to crisp white wines, Sauvignon Blanc isn’t the only game in town. Italian white varieties are on the rise in Sonoma County — and the offerings go way beyond Pinot Grigio.

The delicious proof was on full display at this year’s North Coast Wine Challenge. Competing in the sweepstakes round for top honors were two Sonoma County Italians: a Fiano from DaVero Farms & Winery and a Biancolella d’Ischia from Orsi Family Vineyards.

The trend comes as no surprise to local winemakers like Sam Bilbro. He’s the founder and winemaker at Idlewild Wines in Healdsburg, which specializes in Italian-inspired wines.

“Italian varietals offer such a diversity of flavor profiles and joyful food friendliness,” says Bilbro, who makes wine from a Piedmontese grape called Erbaluce, planted at Las Cimas Ranch on the western edge of Russian River Valley.

“One of the qualities I love about this grape is that it has extreme fresh acidity matched with a textural mouthfeel,” he says. “I find that the aromatics are more driven by mineral tones and fresh Alpine scents with an undertone of orchard fruit.”

Eric Prahl, winemaker at Centennial Mountain Winery in Healdsburg, believes Sonoma County is an especially hospitable place for Italian whites. The Centennial Mountain vineyard includes California’s only planting of Carricante, hailing from Sicily.

“Italian varieties like Carricante have evolved over centuries to maintain balance in warm climates, which makes them highly relevant for the future of Sonoma County,” he says. “They offer a texture and a savory, saline quality that is still relatively uncommon here.”

Bilbro points out that Italian whites grown here sometimes express themselves a little differently in the glass.

“If made in a restrained style,” he says, “I find that Sonoma County is very true to the core of the varietals, as well as showing perhaps just a touch of California sunshine in the fruit tone.”

Three to try

Idlewild Wines

2023 Erbaluce, Las Cimas Vineyard, Russian River Valley, $42

With a vibrant golden color, Idlewild’s Erbaluce combines notes of lemon, fresh herbs and bright acidity. Made without oak, it’s fresh, juicy and food-friendly. 132 Plaza St., Healdsburg, 707-385-9410, idlewildwines.com

Orsi Family Vineyards

2024 Biancolella d’Ischia, Dry Creek Valley, $28

Made from a grape traditionally grown on the island of Ischia, Biancolella is known for its crispness, light body and subtle almond finish. Orsi’s is true to type — a mineral-kissed wine with tropical fruit aromas. 2306 Magnolia Drive, Healdsburg, 707-732-4660, orsifamilyvineyards.com

Centennial Mountain

2022 Carricante, Sonoma County , $49

With a lightly floral aroma, this energetic white shows off notes of citrus, minerals and fresh herbs. Intense, yet full of freshness and zing. It is delicious now, but you could also lay it down for a couple years to see how it develops. 337 Healdsburg Ave., Healdsburg, 669-240-5611, cmvineyard.com

title: Sonoma County Gas Stations Pumping Out Great Grub
summary:
Here are some Sonoma County gas stations with food options that may make the price at the pump a little easier to swallow.

The post Sonoma County Gas Stations Pumping Out Great Grub appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
It’s summertime, which means road trips and hungry travelers clamoring for quick eats. Sure, there are drive-ins, but there are some unexpected surprises at full service fuel shops where you can fill up your car and your belly. We’re not talking about sad hot dogs spinning on roller grills.

Here are some Sonoma County gas stations whose food options may make the price at the pump a little easier to swallow.

Wine Country Café & Deli

Stop in at the Fast Fill Market and Gulf station and treat yourself to the marvelous from-scratch scones, organic apple hand pies, all-day breakfast (smoked salmon croissant!) and plump, made-to-order sandwiches (legit banh mi and coffee-rubbed barbecue tri-tip). Spring through autumn finds barbecue, smashburgers, or street taco pop-ups every Friday in the parking lot. 5855 Sonoma Highway, Santa Rosa. 707-230-2462, winecountrycafedeli.toast.site

Husary 76

Its website lists it as a “convenience store,” but besides diesel and propane, you’ll discover gourmet grub such as real-deal Mexican hot chocolate, and — get this — a countertop wine fridge filled with olive oil crafted from a grove of trees nearby. Station owner and lifelong Sonoma County resident Mousa Husary looked to his Palestinian roots for planting his orchards and producing award-winning extra-virgin cold-pressed olive oil. 2110 Gravenstein Highway N., Sebastopol. 707-829-8252, husaryoliveoil.com

Bonneau Country

A gas station that has its own website with a category titled “cuisine”? This is Wine Country, after all. Find snacks and an early-morning drive-thru barista window at the station’s northern outpost at Arnold Drive and Grove Street. Five miles south at the roundabout, where Highway 116 meets Highway 121, the Carneros Deli just across the parking lot from the fueling and electric charging stations is the place for made-to-order delights: hot and cold sandwiches built from fancy stuff like premium prosciutto, provolone, all the fixings, and an array of breads and spreads including the must-have “spicy boom boom” sauce. 19080 Arnold Drive and 23001 Arnold Drive, Sonoma. 707-939-1646, bonneaucountry.com

Fuel & Food Market

The calling card is the Krispy Krunchy Chicken sign, beckoning you in for the cult-favorite hand-battered bird, the real discovery, though, is the under-the-radar Indian market filled with pantry staples like lentils, rice, and spices ranging from cardamom to black mustard seed. Even the frozen food is a step-up from ordinary, including naan, samosas and kulfi, an Indian specialty similar to ice cream. 4856 Old Redwood Highway, Santa Rosa. 707-843-4083

Vinoma Tapas Argentina

It’s not technically within a gas station, yet beckons from the adjacent Shell parking lot a few steps away. And you would be hard-pressed to find better fast-casual empanadas. These golden-brown Argentinian treats are stuffed with goodness like traditional spiced beef, a vegan curry tofu, or specialties like the plum, bacon, fontina and mozzarella open-faced version called canastita. 5085 Redwood Drive, Rohnert Park. 707-536-9215, vinoma.net

title: Inside Carrusel, Santa Rosa’s Over-The-Top Pink Bruncheria
summary:
Carrusel owner Ivy Reyes has transformed a childhood dream into an over-the-top Santa Rosa bruncheria filled with pink velvet, carousel horses and playful Mexi-brunch dishes.

The post Inside Carrusel, Santa Rosa’s Over-The-Top Pink Bruncheria appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Santa Rosa’s newest — and pinkest — brunch spot began with Ivy Reyes’ childhood dream of owning an Easy-Bake Oven.

Though her family couldn’t afford one, Reyes never forgot the toy oven or her dream of opening a bakery. Decades later, she opened Carrusel, a portal to her youth and a fantasyland of glitter, bows, flowers and carousel horses that makes Barbie’s Dreamhouse look restrained.

“My childhood is poured into here,” Reyes said.

Dressed head to toe in sparkles and sipping a pink Red Bull at 11 a.m. on a Wednesday (what else would she drink?), Reyes radiates Barbie glamour. At 33, the Instagram influencer, who drives a pink Range Rover and dreams up elaborate social media promotions, is very much queen of all she surveys.

“This is just me,” she said, wrapping manicured pink nails around the heart-shaped straw in her energy drink. “I put it together for the love of food, color and a dream. I want it to be an enchantment.”

These days, Reyes is no longer dreaming about an Easy-Bake Oven. She’s overseeing a staff of 50, an ambitious cocktail program and a six-page Mexi-brunch menu that keeps the kitchen busy.

Family roots

Beneath the spectacle is a family story built on work and sacrifice.

Reyes, her immigrant parents and two brothers shared a one-bedroom apartment while the family built La Fondita restaurant and Elenita’s food truck in Roseland. She grew up alongside her mother in the kitchen, learning both the food and business sides of the restaurant industry.

“Growing up, it was very, very worrisome when my parents were starting out and living check to check,” she said. “I remember that, and it keeps me humble.”

Her mother eventually gave Reyes the opportunity to build something of her own, transforming the former La Fondita downtown into something entirely new.

“She put everything on a silver platter,” Reyes said. “From there, she said, ‘Fly with it. You’re on your own.’”

Reyes had hoped her grandmother would be the first person through Carrusel’s doors. Before she died, Reyes showed her the nearly finished restaurant by phone from the hospital and received her blessing.

“I’ve had people of all ages tear up here,” Reyes said. “It brings out the inner child in everyone.”

Flowers, candles and bright colors had always lifted her spirits, and she wanted Carrusel to offer guests the same escape.

“When your world goes gray, paint it pink,” she said. “You can have a bad day, come in here and forget the problems you’re having.”

Best bets

Carrusel is about fun and fantasy rather than fine dining. Expect cotton-candy-topped cocktails, tacos served on a high wire and a Mexi-brunch menu that blends American and Latin flavors with carnival flair. Desserts lean unapologetically sweet, with glazes, marshmallows and chocolate piled high.

And yes, you can eat on the outdoor carousel, which somehow makes everything taste more fun.

Raspberry Mocha Truffle, $8: The fact that I’ve ordered this three times says plenty about my weakness for sugar, glitter and caffeine. Thick raspberry foam (banana and blueberry are also available), edible butterflies (I use “edible” loosely) and chocolatey iced mocha make this a memorable way to start the day. Or night.

Queso Birria Tacos, $20: One of the menu’s most entertaining presentations, with three consommé-soaked birria tacos suspended on a clothesline-like rack. Fiery avocado salsa and extra consommé for dipping complete the show.

Enmoladas, $20: Not the prettiest dish on the menu, but one of the most satisfying. Rich, dark mole blankets chicken-filled tortillas. Sometimes no glitter is needed.

Brunch Board, $35: Order this butterfly-shaped board simply because you can. It comes loaded with banana French toast, strawberry-topped pancakes, a berry-topped Belgian waffle, fresh fruit and Nutella.

Funnel Cake, $18: This fairground favorite is available year-round, piled high with fruit, powdered sugar, chocolate and bananas whenever the craving strikes.

Japanese Pancakes, $18: These take about 20 minutes to make and involve a special technique known only to the kitchen. They aren’t quite as airy as the versions popularized in Japan, but they’re close enough.

Cloud Nine, $18: Dragon berry rum, lychee, lemon and vanilla topped with a cloud of cotton candy — exactly what your 9-year-old self imagined you would be drinking at 21.

Mimosa Flight, $38: Every mimosa should come this way. More brunchy fun for everyone.

Chilaquiles, $19: Judging by the number landing on neighboring tables, this may be the restaurant’s most popular dish.

Open from 7 a.m. to 10 p.m. daily. Carrusel is at 630 Third St., Santa Rosa, 707-655-8365, instagram.com/cafe_carrusel.

title: Saucy Mama’s Jook Joint in Guerneville is the Spot People Plan Vacations Around
summary:
Yvette Bidegain carries on her father’s barbecue legacy with catfish, ribs, fried chicken and plenty of personality at Saucy Mama’s Jook Joint.

The post Saucy Mama’s Jook Joint in Guerneville is the Spot People Plan Vacations Around appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Yvette Bidegain thought she knew what Californians wanted to eat. Okra and catfish weren’t on the list.

Four years after opening Saucy Mama’s Jook Joint in Guerneville, they’re her two best-selling dishes.

“I used to sneak catfish to my friends’ table because they really wanted it,” she said. Other diners noticed and started asking for it, too. Eventually, the farm-raised catfish earned a permanent place on the menu.

Saucy Mama’s is equal parts soul food restaurant, neighborhood hangout, birthday destination and post-river stop, wrapped in a barbecue-roadhouse-meets-New Orleans aesthetic.

Tucked along a bend in Highway 116 west of downtown Guerneville, it’s the kind of place many drivers pass on their way to the coast. Yet Saucy Mama’s is almost always full, with Bidegain greeting guests and keeping the dining room humming. Some regulars even plan vacations around getting a “Saucy Mama fix.”

Bidegain’s menu blends the Southern cooking of her family’s Louisiana and Mississippi roots with her own California sensibility. Since opening in 2022, the restaurant has built a loyal following.

The backstory

Bidegain is the daughter of Leroy Richardson, whose Richardson’s Ribs was a Sonoma County Fair favorite in the 1980s and ’90s before expanding into restaurants in Santa Rosa and Sebastopol. His recipes remain the backbone of Saucy Mama’s menu.

At first, Bidegain resisted leaning on the family name.

“I didn’t want to take my dad’s name down with me,” she said.

Then her mother tasted Bidegain’s gumbo and delivered the compliment that mattered most: “Baby, your gumbo tastes just like your daddy’s.”

She knew she was onto something.

Richardson’s recipes live on in Bidegain’s kitchen, while signs, menus, family photographs and other mementos from his restaurants cover the walls.

Not every dish would have earned her father’s approval. Bidegain jokes he’s probably rolling over in his grave over the tofu po’ boy and meatless succotash.

Even the restaurant’s bright red smoker felt like fate. Bidegain had gone to a restaurant supply store looking for a sink and instead found a used Texas smoker she’d long pined for — marked down to half price.

“A lot of things happened like that for us,” she said. “I truly think my father was orchestrating it from heaven.”

Here’s what to know before you go.

Yvette’s favorite dish

Pork ribs.

Fun fact

Bidegain didn’t like soul food growing up. While her friends ate spaghetti with Parmesan, she dreaded collard greens, neck bones and black-eyed peas.

That changed in her 20s, when she started cooking for herself. During her pregnancy, she found herself craving the dishes she’d once avoided.

“It’s just in my DNA,” she said. “Your blood takes over.”

The vibe

You will not get in without a reservation, so don’t try to sweet-talk Bidegain, who is usually at the front door greeting guests. When the restaurant is full, it’s full.

The crowd ranges from birthday celebrants in dress clothes to river-goers in flip-flops, and nobody looks out of place.

Inside, Saucy Mama’s is a joyful jumble of vintage New Orleans signs, memorabilia from Richardson’s restaurants, Black art and hundreds of donated knickknacks. Maximalist hardly begins to describe it.

Every holiday brings another round of decorations. “Restraint” is not in her vocabulary. Bidegain originally envisioned a true jook joint with live music and dancing, but the restaurant became so popular there’s barely room between the tables.

The food

Come hungry. Portions are generous, and nobody comes here to count calories.

Crispy fried catfish entree, $20: The seasoned cornmeal crust is crisp and flavorful, without the heavy, bready coating that can sink lesser catfish. Inside, the farm-raised fish is moist, succulent and clean-tasting.

Shrimp po’ boy, $22: A small French loaf is cut into a boat rather than sliced through, holding a messy pile of fried shrimp, lettuce, tomatoes and remoulade.

Buttermilk fried chicken entree, $25: The boldly seasoned crust fries up crisp, giving way to juicy meat. Pair it with red beans and rice and collard greens for the soul food holy trinity. The loose bits of crunchy crust left on the plate are worth chasing with a fork. Served with cornbread waffles, crack butter and two sides.

Barbecue pork ribs entree, $28: Coated in Bidegain’s secret dry rub for at least 24 hours before spending hours in the smoker, the ribs are deeply smoky and tender. They’re slathered in a sweet barbecue sauce and best eaten with plenty of napkins. Served with cornbread waffles, crack butter and two sides.

Extras, $8: Great barbecue restaurants live or die by their sides. Here, the macaroni and cheese — made with four cheeses and cream — is rich and satisfying. The standout, though, is the fried okra tossed with onions and bacon.

All meats are available à la carte, including a full rack of pork ribs and fried chicken.

Banana pudding, $6: Even banana pudding skeptics may be won over by this version, layered into a shortbread crust and topped with whipped cream.

The menu also includes several gluten-free and vegetarian options, along with beer, cider, wine and nonalcoholic drinks.

The discount

Because Bidegain spent years as a Caltrans equipment operator, she offers a 10% discount to fellow operating engineers.

The spot

16632 Highway 116, Guerneville, 707-604-7184, saucymamasjookjoint.com

title: Bay Area Designer’s Cape Dutch-Style Home Hits the Market in Glen Ellen
summary:
The Glen Ellen home references traditional architecture from South Africa’s acclaimed wine region and includes whimsical touches like cast-iron street lamps and a British phone booth.

content:
A Glen Ellen home with Cape Dutch style is currently listed for sale. The farmhouse, guest house, barn-style office and pool on 16 acres is currently seeking $12,000,000.

The home is the work of resident and designer Patrick Printy — a veteran style-maker for major brands, such as Levi’s and Restoration Hardware, and lead of his own firm with projects published in magazines from Elle Decor to House Beautiful. 

This particular three-bedroom, three-bathroom farmhouse references traditional architecture from South Africa’s wine country. A unique design for the Sonoma area, the dwelling has the signature Cape Dutch scalloped, ornamented gables. Inside, there’s handcrafted Dutch cabinetry by Johannes Van Mourik and also handmade Dutch “witjes” tiles.

Use of grandly sized oak wood beams and floor planks, reclaimed from Midwestern barns, creates dramatic farm character throughout. The property’s exterior stonework was sourced from rocks quarried from the property.

Eclectic textiles create a cohesive but collected look. The interiors are an impossibly successful mix of old and new, clean-lined and traditional with pleasing dollops of fun tossed in. This is exemplified right at the front door where black-and-white traditional symmetry is made playful with the addition of wonderfully “matchy” Dalmatian statues. Vintage cast-iron street lamps, sourced from San Francisco’s China Basin, and a British phone booth offer spectacular whimsy to the grounds.

The grounds include a pond, a well and solar panels. There are two additional parcels for future development.

title: Sebastopol’s Famous Monte-Bellaria Estate and Lavender Farm for Sale
summary:
Boasting over 38,000 lavender plants, Monte-Bellaria has long drawn visitors with its rich sensory experience and handmade lavender products. Now the farm and hilltop home is on the market.

The post Sebastopol’s Famous Monte-Bellaria Estate and Lavender Farm for Sale appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
A Sebastopol estate with a lavender farm — one of the largest in northern California — is currently listed for sale. A four-bedroom, three-and-half-bathroom home on 14 acres with 38,000 lavender plants, an olive orchard, apiary and farm store are listed for $4,995,000.

The property, named Monte-Bellaria — meaning “mountain of beautiful air” in Italian — has been a beloved stop along the Sonoma County Farm Trails. The land, stewarded since 2002 by the late Dr. Bill MacElroy, has sloping rows of the hardy and fragrant Grosso lavender plant.

Yearly, MacElroy, along with farm manager and beekeeper Eric Silas, cultivated and harvested the lavender, from which he would distill the essential oils to create the property’s popular products: soaps, balms, hydrosols and a sumptuous lavender honey. The handmade goods, including olive oils made from the yields of their orchard, were sold at the on-site farm store. Monte-Bellaria became a popular site for visitors seeking tranquility, a bit of shopping and a swoon-worthy photo backdrop.

A walk through the grounds is a rich sensory experience. In addition to the immense fragrance during high bloom season, there’s a sound bath of buzzing from the bees hard at work pollinating the plants. 

The 4,965-square-foot hilltop home, built in 2014, takes style cues from the Tuscan countryside, which inspired MacElroy’s development of the farm. The dwelling is airy with high ceilings, lime-washed walls in earth tones, walnut-stained millwork and natural stone. Plentiful windows offer sweeping views of lavender and neighboring vineyards.

Amenities include an additional prep kitchen, an elevator and an outdoor brick oven. A secondary unit is a tranquil spot with the same luxury finishes.
